title: Leopold Aschenbrenner and the Wall Street lesson every genius learns
excerpt: Leopold Aschenbrenner's hedge fund collapse shows how even brilliant investors can get crushed when markets turn.
content_html:
The humbling of Leopold Aschenbrenner: The market doesn't care how smart you are.

By Alistair Barr

You're currently following this author! Want to unfollow? Unsubscribe via the link in your email.

Author of the Tech Memo newsletter

Leopold Aschenbrenner is one of the most knowledgeable people in AI. But he was just schooled on a fundamental Wall Street truth: Being the smartest person in the room doesn't stop you from getting your face ripped off. In fact, sometimes it helps get you there.

On Thursday, Ken Griffin's Citadel bought a portion of the public stock portfolio owned by Aschenbrenner's hedge fund, Situational Awareness, after the fund suffered steep losses during the recent selloff in AI stocks. Situational Awareness is keeping its private investments, including a stake in Anthropic, but a chunk of its public equity portfolio is now in Citadel's hands.

Traders really do call it "getting your face ripped off." Griffin was the one doing it this time. I would not have wanted to be on that call. Ouch.

This is an extraordinary reversal for a fund that was riding high just a couple of months ago.

Aschenbrenner, a former OpenAI researcher, became famous after publishing Situational Awareness, a 165-page essay, in 2024. He argued that artificial intelligence would transform the economy far faster than most people expected.

He predicted trillion-dollar investments in AI computing, huge new data centers, and growing government involvement in the race to build powerful AI systems. Those predictions now look remarkably accurate.

His hedge fund was built around that same conviction, grounded in deep AI knowledge and a network of technical experts he knows across Silicon Valley. The investments concentrated on companies that stood to benefit from the AI boom, from memory-chip makers to infrastructure companies and cloud computing businesses.

The strategy worked spectacularly well. According to the Financial Times, the fund returned 439% during the first half of this year.

Then the market turned. That doesn't necessarily mean Aschenbrenner's ideas are wrong. History suggests something much more uncomfortable.

LTCM's Russia lesson

Wall Street has a long record of punishing investors who were fundamentally right, and believed in their vision intensely, but couldn't survive long enough to prove it.

The classic example is Long-Term Capital Management. This hedge fund was run by some of the smartest people in finance, including Nobel Prize-winning economists. It built sophisticated trades based on the belief that certain price differences in markets would eventually disappear. The logic behind many of those trades was sound.

Then Russia defaulted on its debt in 1998. Markets stopped behaving the way the models expected. Long-Term Capital Management had borrowed heavily to increase its returns, and those borrowings became its downfall. As losses mounted, lenders demanded more cash. Other traders realized the fund would eventually be forced to sell and traded against its positions. The fund ultimately required a rescue organized by the Federal Reserve to prevent broader financial damage.

The market didn't stop to ask whether the fund's ideas were clever. It simply asked who needed to sell first.

Clarium's oil lesson

Peter Thiel's Clarium Capital tells a similar story. In the mid-2000s, his hedge fund built large positions around a bold view that oil prices were headed much higher. For a time, that looked like a brilliant call. Then energy markets reversed. Thiel suffered huge losses and his fund shrank dramatically.

Like Long-Term Capital Management before it, Clarium discovered that a strong investment thesis is not the same thing as a winning trade. If markets move against you before your ideas play out, conviction becomes a liability instead of an advantage.

Situational Awareness now joins that list. According to the Financial Times, the fund used borrowing to increase the size of its bets, a common hedge-fund strategy that boosts returns in good times, but magnifies losses when markets fall.

One theory

The immediate trigger for the recent selloff may have had little to do with Aschenbrenner's long-term vision for AI.

Here's one potential theory. Memory-chip stocks in South Korea were hit by heavy selling starting in June, which triggered margin calls. A margin call happens when investors borrow money to buy stocks and those investments fall so much that lenders demand either more cash or the sale of assets to repay part of the loan.

Many Korean traders had bought AI stocks on margin, so this created a vicious cycle. Investors sell to meet the margin call. Prices fall further. More investors receive margin calls. They sell too. Before long, the selling spreads well beyond the original stocks and starts pulling down anything that looks similar.

Many of the AI stocks owned by Situational Awareness sat squarely in that part of the market. Whether Aschenbrenner remained convinced about AI no longer mattered. Traders had to sell on the market's timetable.

This forced selling may have hit some of Aschenbrenner's holdings. When the fund suffered big losses, he may also have been forced to sell to unwind the leverage he'd been using. This ultimately ended with a massive sale of its book of public stock to Citadel. A spokesman for Aschenbrenner didn't immediately comment on the record.

Tuesday's market action suggests this is exactly what happened. After news broke that Citadel had acquired much of Situational Awareness' public portfolio, several AI-related stocks linked to the fund rallied sharply, including Sandisk and Nebius. Investors appear to have concluded that one of the biggest forced sellers has finally disappeared.

Ironically, some of Aschenbrenner's favorite stocks may now recover after he has been forced out of them.

That's one of the cruelest features of financial markets. You can correctly identify one of the biggest fundamental shifts of your generation. You can understand an industry better than almost anyone else. You can even build exactly the right portfolio. But if you add enough leverage and enough conviction, the market eventually stops judging your ideas. It starts judging your ability to survive.

Long-Term Capital Management learned that lesson. Clarium learned it. Now Situational Awareness has learned it, too.

content_html_zh:
利奥波德·阿申布伦纳 (Leopold Aschenbrenner) 的谦卑：市场并不关心你有多聪明。

作者：Alistair Barr 您目前正在关注该作者！ 想要取消关注吗？ 通过电子邮件中的链接取消订阅。 《技术备忘录》时事通讯的作者

Leopold Aschenbrenner 是人工智能领域知识最渊博的人之一。 但他只是接受了华尔街的一个基本真理：成为房间里最聪明的人并不能阻止你的脸被撕掉。 事实上，有时它可以帮助你实现目标。

周四，肯·格里芬 (Ken Griffin) 的 Citadel 购买了阿申布伦纳 (Aschenbrenner) 的对冲基金 Situational Awareness 所拥有的部分公开股票投资组合，此前该基金在最近人工智能股票的抛售中遭受了巨大损失。 Situational Awareness 保留其私人投资，包括 Anthropic 的股份，但其公共股权投资组合的很大一部分现在掌握在 Citadel 手中。

交易员确实称之为“让你的脸被撕掉”。 这次是格里芬干的。 我本来不想参加那个电话会议。 哎哟。

对于几个月前还处于高位的基金来说，这是一次非同寻常的逆转。

Aschenbrenner 是前 OpenAI 研究员，因 2024 年发表 165 页的论文《态势感知》而名声大噪。 他认为人工智能改变经济的速度远远快于大多数人的预期。

他预测人工智能计算、庞大的新数据中心以及政府越来越多地参与构建强大人工智能系统的竞赛将有数万亿美元的投资。 现在看来，这些预测非常准确。

他的对冲基金也是围绕同样的信念建立的，以深厚的人工智能知识和他在硅谷认识的技术专家网络为基础。 这些投资集中在那些将从人工智能热潮中受益的公司，从内存芯片制造商到基础设施公司和云计算企业。

该策略的效果非常好。 据英国《金融时报》报道，该基金今年上半年的回报率为 439%。

然后市场发生了逆转。 这并不一定意味着阿申布伦纳的想法是错误的。 历史表明了一些更令人不舒服的事情。

LTCM 的俄罗斯课程

华尔街长期以来一直惩罚那些基本正确、坚信自己愿景的投资者，但却无法生存足够长的时间来证明这一点。

典型的例子是长期资本管理。 该对冲基金由一些金融界最聪明的人经营，其中包括诺贝尔奖获得者经济学家。 它建立了复杂的交易，其基础是相信市场中的某些价格差异最终会消失。 其中许多交易背后的逻辑都是合理的。

1998年，俄罗斯出现债务违约。 市场不再按照模型预期的方式表现。 长期资本管理公司为了增加回报而大量举债，而这些借款却导致了它的垮台。 随着损失的增加，贷款人要求更多的现金。 其他交易员意识到该基金最终将被迫出售并与其头寸进行交易。 该基金最终需要美联储组织救援，以防止更广泛的财务损失。

市场并没有停下来询问该基金的想法是否聪明。 它只是问谁需要先出售。

Clarium 精油课程

Peter Thiel 的 Clarium Capital 也讲述了类似的故事。 2000 年代中期，他的对冲基金基于油价将大幅上涨的大胆观点建立了大量头寸。 有一段时间，这看起来像是一个绝妙的决定。 随后能源市场出现逆转。 蒂尔遭受了巨大损失，他的基金也大幅缩水。

与之前的长期资本管理公司一样，Clarium 发现强有力的投资理论并不等同于成功的交易。 如果在你的想法付诸实践之前市场对你不利，信念就会变成一种负担而不是优势。

态势感知现在也加入了这个列表。 据英国《金融时报》报道，该基金利用借款来增加押注规模，这是一种常见的对冲基金策略，可以在经济繁荣时提高回报，但在市场下跌时放大损失。

一种理论

近期抛售的直接触发因素可能与阿申布伦纳对人工智能的长期愿景没有多大关系。

这是一种潜在的理论。 韩国内存芯片股从 6 月份开始遭遇大量抛售，引发追加保证金通知。 当投资者借钱购买股票，而这些投资大幅下跌，以至于贷款人要求更多现金或出售资产来偿还部分贷款时，就会发生追加保证金通知。

许多韩国交易员以保证金购买了人工智能股票，因此这就形成了恶性循环。 投资者卖出以满足追加保证金通知。 价格进一步下跌。 更多投资者收到追加保证金通知。 他们也卖。 不久之后，抛售范围远远超出了原来的股票，并开始拉低任何看起来相似的股票。

Situational Awareness 拥有的许多人工智能股票正好位于该市场的一部分。 阿申布伦纳是否仍然相信人工智能已经不再重要。 交易员必须按照市场时间表出售。

这次被迫抛售可能影响了阿申布伦纳的部分持股。 当该基金遭受重大损失时，他也可能被迫出售以平仓他一直使用的杠杆。 最终，该公司将其公开股票大量出售给 Citadel。 阿申布伦纳的发言人没有立即对此发表评论。

周二的市场走势表明这正是所发生的情况。 在 Citadel 收购了 Situational Awareness 大部分公开投资组合的消息传出后，与该基金相关的几只人工智能相关股票大幅上涨，其中包括 Sandisk 和 Nebius。 投资者似乎得出结论，最大的被迫抛售者之一终于消失了。

具有讽刺意味的是，阿申布伦纳最喜欢的一些股票在他被迫退出后现在可能会反弹。
